name: Zane Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for coming in, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Anything you say here is confidential. All right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, no worries. I'm not much of a talker, so you'll have to dig a bit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Happy to. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the shearer on a longwall at an underground coal mine. The shearer is a big machine with two cutting drums that rides along a coal face about three hundred metres wide, shaving off a slice each pass, and the roof supports walk forward behind it. I'm the senior operator on my shift, so I set the cutting speed, watch the gas readings and keep the young ones from doing anything stupid. It's loud, it's wet and it's hot, and I like it, because when the face is running sweet you can cut eight thousand tonnes in a shift. What I don't like is the paperwork that's crept in over the years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much. Maybe that I never trusted it anyway. I don't post online, so it'd just be a few words in the bathhouse after shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doesn't mean much for me. The longwall doesn't care what's trending on the internet. It cuts coal or it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep cutting coal, keep putting money in the offset account on the house, and maybe buy a second-hand boat in summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as every other week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI at all, even on your phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My sister set one up on my phone and I deleted it. I don't need a computer telling me how to write a text message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in a year in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same face, same crew, probably a couple of tonnes faster because the new roof supports came in. I'd have the house nearly paid off.

S0.say: He wouldn't say much, maybe that he never trusted AI anyway. He doesn't post online, so it'd be a few words in the bathhouse after shift.
S0.think: He thinks it means little for him, because the longwall cuts coal regardless of what's trending online. Underground life wouldn't change.
S0.do: Keeps cutting coal and paying money into the offset account on his house. Considers buying a second-hand boat in summer.
S0.quote: The longwall doesn't care what's trending on the internet.
S0.fieldNote: Zane is short-spoken and grounded in the physical machine. He has actively rejected AI tools, deleting one his sister installed. His plans are small and concrete, built around paying off his house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they've been trying to automate longwalls for twenty years, and we're still down there. A computer doesn't know when the roof's about to come in. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not a lot changes underground for a while. The office side might get cut, the planners, the surveyors. Down the pit it's still dirty and unpredictable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and wait to see what they actually bring in. If they wanted me trained on something, I'd do it on their time. I'm not spending my days off on a computer course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a bit irritated by all the talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Longwalls are already partly automated in some places. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Our shearer already follows the face on its own for part of a pass, it remembers the cut from the last run. They call it automation, but I still have to stand beside it and tell it it's wrong twice a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your mine changed, would you go to another one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sure. There are three other mines within an hour's drive, and they're always short of good shearer operators. If one went robot-heavy I'd just go to another one that hadn't.

S1.say: He'd say longwall automation has been coming for twenty years and miners are still down there, because a computer doesn't know when the roof is about to come in.
S1.think: He expects office jobs like planning and surveying to be cut before anything changes much underground. Down the pit it stays dirty and unpredictable.
S1.do: Keeps doing his job and waits to see what's brought in, training only on company time. Would switch to one of three nearby mines if his became too automated.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a bit irritated by all the talk.
S1.quote: They call it automation, but I still have to stand beside it and tell it it's wrong twice a shift.
S1.fieldNote: Zane's confidence rests on underground conditions being too messy for machines, backed by everyday experience correcting the semi-automated shearer. Plenty of nearby mines give him an easy exit. He won't learn new tools on his own time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they'd better make sure it works first. If a robot cuts into a gas pocket and the whole thing goes up, people die. I'd say slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if it's real, I'm done for. All my skills are about one machine in one kind of mine. I don't know how to do anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending, full stop. No boat, no new truck. I'd put everything into the house so it's paid off, then sit on the rest and see how it pans out. I wouldn't know what else to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the roof's creaking and you can't see where.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to another mine. Does that still work here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If every mine's got the same robots, there's nowhere to go. I've never been anything but a miner, not even for a summer. My whole family works in the pits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first money decision you'd make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off the house. If I own the roof over my head, I can live on not much for a long time.

S2.say: He'd say they'd better be sure it works, because a robot cutting into a gas pocket could kill people. He'd tell them to slow down.
S2.think: He thinks if it's real he's finished, because his skills are tied to one machine in one kind of mine.
S2.do: Stops all spending, dropping the boat and a new truck. Pays off the house first and then holds the rest of his savings while he waits to see what happens.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like hearing the roof creak without knowing where.
S2.quote: If every mine's got the same robots, there's nowhere to go. I've never been anything but a miner, not even for a summer.
S2.fieldNote: His easy exit to other mines disappears in this picture and with it his calm. Without any plan B, his only move is to secure his house and wait. He has never worked outside mining, and neither has his family, so there's no other identity to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, just slower. Make sure it's safe, and give people time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still bad, but I'd have the house done and a bit of money, so I wouldn't be on the street. Five years of good pay is a lot of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work every overtime shift going for the first couple of years and get the house paid off by thirty. Then I'd look at something with my hands that's slow to change, maybe going in with my uncle on his earthmoving business. I'd still be watching, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's real, but I'd have time to get my feet under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years puts you at thirty-two. Would you change jobs before it hits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in year three or four. My uncle runs a couple of excavators doing house sites. It's not the money, it's that I don't know who I am if I'm not underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you vote differently in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote for whoever looks like they'd slow it down a bit. I'm not big on politics either way. Just someone sensible.

S3.say: He'd say the same as in the fast picture, only slower. Make sure the machines are safe underground, and give people time to adjust.
S3.think: He thinks it's still bad, but he'd own his house and have savings, so he wouldn't be on the street.
S3.do: Works every overtime shift in the first couple of years to pay off his house by 30. Around year three or four, considers joining his uncle's earthmoving business doing house sites.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with time to get his footing.
S3.quote: It's not the money, it's that I don't know who I am if I'm not underground.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Zane's plan becomes to bank as much as possible and then move to his uncle's small earthmoving business. The real fear he names is losing who he is, not money. His politics stay middle-of-the-road and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time. Lots can happen, lots can go wrong with it. I wouldn't believe it until I saw it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that I'll get most of my career in before it hits. I'd be thirty-seven, house paid, savings in the bank. Not great, but survivable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much different in year one. I'd keep working, keep paying the house down, maybe go easier on the toys. I'd wait three or four years to see how fast it's really going before I did anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's far enough away I can not think about it most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in year one than you do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, really. Ten years out, I'd treat it like the weather forecast for next month: interesting, not something you dress for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safe-ish. The house is the safe bit. The rest I'd figure out when it's closer.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a long time and lots can go wrong, so he wouldn't believe it until he saw it.
S4.think: He thinks he'll get most of his career in before it hits and be 37 with a paid-off house and savings, which is survivable.
S4.do: Keeps working and paying down the house in year one, spending less on toys. Waits three or four years to see how fast it really moves before doing anything big.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but far enough off to ignore most days.
S4.quote: Ten years out, I'd treat it like the weather forecast for next month: interesting, not something you dress for.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Zane return to his default of waiting it out. His house is his anchor across every scenario. He'd act only once he could see the change with his own eyes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have nowhere to go. What would help is time, really, and some kind of payout that lets people like me get the house paid off and work out the next thing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss the smell of a fresh-cut coal face, and I know that sounds mad to anyone who's never been down there. That's it.

headlineQuote: I'd miss the smell of a fresh-cut coal face, and I know that sounds mad to anyone who's never been down there.
portrait: Zane Evans is 27, the senior shearer operator on a longwall at an underground coal mine, single and paying off his own house. He is short-spoken, distrusts AI tools and believes underground conditions are too messy for machines to take over soon, and he knows three other mines nearby would hire him. He stays calm through AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, becomes alarmed when AGI arrives in two years and leaves him nowhere to go, and is anxious and then uneasy with five or ten years. Across the AGI pictures his first move is to pay off the house, and with time he'd consider joining his uncle's earthmoving business.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there would be no other mine to go to.
whatWouldHelp: Time, and a payout big enough to let workers like him pay off their homes and work out what to do next.
